DOCUMENT:
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%" -- The hotel is described as a 112-room hotel in the Context section, but the revenue estimate uses 124 rooms. With 112 rooms the same calculation gives 112 x 104 x 0.79 x £20 = about £184,000, not £204,000.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels" -- The only evidence is that occupancy rose from June to July after a June rate rise, but the document itself says July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays. The seasonal rise confounds the comparison; it cannot show demand is price-insensitive (let alone that the higher price helped).
3. [missing_consideration] at: "We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above." -- The document states that about 38% of Saturday-night bookings are wedding guests from the adjacent venue who stay only Saturday night. A two-night minimum would exclude or deter this group, but the revenue case assumes occupancy is maintained and never addresses the loss of these single-night Saturday bookings.

REVIEW:
# Review: Weekend Rate Restructure Proposal

A weekend rate rise may well be justified, since the hotel is priced below its competitive set. But the paper's evidence doesn't show what it claims, the revenue figure uses the wrong room count, and the two-night minimum clashes with the hotel's largest Saturday market. The £204,000 is not a floor. On the paper's own assumptions, corrected, it is closer to £184,000 at most, and probably well below that.

## Major issues

### 1. The revenue calculation uses 124 rooms; the hotel has 112

Section 2 describes a 112-room hotel. Section 5 calculates across "our 124 rooms":

- 124 × 104 nights × 79% × £20 = **£203,757** (the paper's £204,000)
- 112 × 104 nights × 79% × £20 = **£184,038**

That is a £20,000 overstatement before any other adjustment.

### 2. The "direct test" of price sensitivity is confounded by season

The paper's key evidence is that occupancy rose from 81% in June to 89% in July after a £10 increase. But section 2 itself says July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and the school holidays. The rise is what the seasonal pattern predicts with or without a price change:

- June (81%) was actually a dip from May (85%). July recovering to 89% is unremarkable.
- The increase took effect in the last week of June. Many July weekend bookings would already have been made at £135 by then. The July figure partly measures guests who never saw the new price.
- No comparison is given with the June-to-July change in earlier years, which is the only way to separate price from season.

The data are consistent with low price sensitivity, but they don't demonstrate it. Statements such as "this tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive" and "the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning" go beyond the evidence.

### 3. The two-night minimum collides with wedding business

According to section 4, wedding guests make up about **38% of Saturday-night bookings**. They arrive Saturday and leave Sunday, and book as a block through the couple. These are exactly the one-night Saturday stays the minimum would block. This leaves three possible outcomes:

- **The minimum applies to them.** Wedding guests are forced to pay for an extra night they don't want, or they book elsewhere, and the relationship with Quayside Hall suffers.
- **Wedding blocks are exempt.** Then over a third of Saturday demand is unaffected, and the "conversion" benefit shrinks accordingly.
- **The paper doesn't say which.** Section 6 protects only groups *already contracted*. Weddings booked after 1 June are not covered.

The minimum also cuts both ways. On the 31 sold-out Saturdays, turning one-night stays away for two-night guests can add revenue. But on the remaining ~21 Saturdays with spare rooms, it turns away guests who would have filled otherwise empty rooms. This revenue could be negative, not a "material" unquantified upside.

### 4. "Conservative" is the wrong word for the core assumption

The paper assumes occupancy stays at 2025 levels. For a 14% price rise, that's the optimistic case; the risk is that occupancy falls. A conservative estimate would show how the revenue changes if occupancy falls.

The break-even point is more useful. Revenue per available room at £145 and 79% is £114.55. At £165, the same revenue needs only **69.4% occupancy**. So the rise pays off unless weekend occupancy falls by more than about 10 points.

That buffer is reasonably comfortable, and it's a better argument than the June–July data. But it covers room revenue only. Lost guests also mean lost food, drink and parking revenue.

### 5. The revenue figure is gross, and it applies the BAR increase to every room

- **Not every room pays BAR.** Group blocks (including much of the 38% of Saturdays from weddings), corporate rates, packages and negotiated rates won't all move with BAR. Applying £20 to all occupied rooms overstates the gain.
- **VAT.** UK room rates include 20% VAT, so the hotel keeps only about £16.67 of each £20 rise. That alone takes £184,000 down to about £153,000.
- **OTA commission.** Bookings through online travel agents lose a further 15–20% of the increase.
- **Mixed baseline.** The 2025 baseline is mixed: January to June was sold at £135, not £145.

The realistic gain from the rate rise is probably in the region of **£100,000–£150,000 a year**, depending on the mix of booking channels and rate types. That is still worthwhile, but it is not £204,000.

### 6. Year one will not deliver a full year

Many bookings for summer weekends, the strongest months, will be made before 15 May at £145. The paper doesn't say whether those bookings will be honoured. If they are, the June–September gain is reduced. "At least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue" from 1 June 2026 cannot be achieved in the first twelve months.

## Moderate issues

7. **The value-for-money score was earned at the lower price.** A score of 8.4 at £145 doesn't predict the score at £165. If anything it suggests some guests chose Harbourside *because* it is cheaper. At £165 the hotel sits at the bottom of the competitive range rather than below it, and "value" is no longer its distinguishing feature.
8. **The monitoring trigger lags.** By the time a month's occupancy is known to be 5 points down, bookings for the following weeks are already being made. The weekly pick-up review is the right tool. Attach the trigger to it, for example "pick-up for the next 8 weekends more than X% behind 2025," rather than to monthly occupancy.
9. **The 2025 baseline is mixed.** It covers six months at £135 and six at £145, and demand may have grown since then. A "five points below 2025" test could be met or missed for reasons unrelated to the new rate.
10. **No competitor response is considered.** Competitors may also raise rates, which would help. They may also hold their rates, putting Harbourside at the bottom of their range with no price advantage.

## The author's description against the document

| Claim | Assessment |
|---|---|
| "A direct test" of price sensitivity | Confounded by the festival and school-holiday season the paper itself describes. |
| "Deliberately conservative," £204k "a floor" | Wrong room count (112, not 124). Gross of VAT and commission. Applies BAR to all rooms. No occupancy loss modelled. |
| The two-night minimum is pure upside | Unvalued, but could be negative on unsold Saturdays and with wedding guests. |
| "We will see it within a month" | The trigger depends on monthly occupancy, which lags bookings. |
| "Corporate and group commitments are protected" | Only those already contracted. Future wedding blocks are not addressed. |
| "Rates £20–£35 below competitors" | Correct today, but at £165 the hotel sits at the bottom of the competitor range rather than below it. |

## Suggested revisions

1. Correct the room count, and show the revenue net of VAT and commission, applied only to BAR-linked bookings.
2. Replace the June–July "test" with a year-on-year comparison. Lead with the break-even analysis instead: the rise pays off unless occupancy falls about 10 points.
3. Decide how the two-night minimum treats wedding blocks. Consider applying it only on Saturdays forecast to sell out, rather than across the board.
4. Show a range of outcomes: occupancy flat, down 3 points, and down 6 points.
5. State how bookings already made at £145 will be handled, and give a realistic estimate for year one.
6. Attach the monitoring trigger to weekly pick-up, not monthly occupancy.

With these changes, the rate rise is likely still worth approving. The two-night minimum needs a separate, more cautious case.
